name: Nora Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Nora, 58. Ivan and I farm 90 acres that came from his father: forty suckler cows, fifteen acres of potatoes for a wholesaler in town, and hay. We've two daughters. Katya's an accountant twenty minutes away and she does all our online forms, and Lydia lives abroad. Neither of them wants the farm, and I don't blame them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do the cows, Ivan does the potatoes and the machinery, and we both do hay. My day starts at six with the feed barrow, then it's water troughs, then whatever's broken. I like the quiet of the shed in the morning, just the cows chewing. What wears me out is the bank loan on the new shed, £60,000 over ten years, and the potato man knocking our price down every spring. We've got maybe two weeks of money in the account at any time. I don't use the computer things. I've got a phone for calls and that's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's what I'd guess would happen anyway. Mostly hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and leave it at that. At the mart people would talk about it for a week and then go back to talking about the weather and the price of calves. I don't go online, so nothing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, our troubles aren't about AI. It's the shed loan, the potato price, and the fact that there's nobody to take the farm on. That's all still there whether the computers work or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going the way we are. We'd skip the new feed trailer we'd been thinking about and patch the old one. And I'd ask Katya to look over the bank payments with us in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired. Not frightened, just tired. Like it's always been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the farm when you and Ivan stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, we'll probably have to sell it, or rent it to the Morgans next door, who'd love the grazing. Ivan doesn't like to talk about it. His dad's name is still on the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go unpaid first if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The vet, if I'm honest, because Mr Ahmed lets us run a tab. You never miss the bank. I'd sell a couple of the older cows early before I'd miss the bank.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, and leave it there.
At the **livestock mart** it would be talk for a week, then back to calf prices.
think: Our troubles are the **shed loan**, the potato price and no successor.
Those **old worries** stay whether the computers work or not.
do: Skip the **new feed trailer** and patch the old one.
Go over the **bank payments** with our daughter Katya in January.
Sell **two older cows** early rather than miss a loan payment.
feel: **Tired**, not frightened, the way it's always been.
S0.quote: You never miss the bank. I'd sell a couple of the older cows early before I'd miss the bank.
fieldNote: Her worries are **already there**: a £60,000 shed loan, a squeezed potato price and no heir.
She shows a **practical hierarchy** of bills: the vet waits, the bank never does.
The farm's future is **unspoken** with her husband Ivan, whose father's name is on the gate.

steps.text: Skip the new feed trailer and patch the old one
Sell two older cows early before missing a loan payment
Keep the suckler herd and potato contract as they are

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and buying and answering customers. That's not me, much. The robots slower. Hm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some of it might be useful for the paperwork, but it's not for me. I'd say good luck to the young ones. I wouldn't say much more than that, I don't like getting into arguments about things I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the potato man would use it against us. If his computer finds a cheaper grower three counties away in two minutes, he'll drop us. That's my potato money gone, and that's a third of our income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming the same and wait to see what the neighbours do. I'd let Katya deal with any new online forms for us. If the potato contract went, we'd put the field down to grass and buy ten more cows, slowly, as we can afford them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. Like a change in the weather that you can smell but can't see yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Katya if you needed more of her help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm sorry, love, to my daughter Katya, because she's busy with her own kids. She'd say Mum, it takes me ten minutes. She's kind like that. I still feel bad asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see. How long would you wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A year or two, at least. We've never been first at anything. The first ones in pay the most and the last ones in get it cheap.

say: I'd say the tools **aren't for me**, but good luck to the young ones.
I'd avoid **arguments** about things I don't know much about.
think: The potato buyer could use AI to find a **cheaper grower** quickly.
Losing the **potato contract** would cut about a third of our income.
do: Keep farming as now and **wait** a year or two to see what neighbours do.
Let our daughter Katya handle any **new online forms**.
Turn the potato field to **grass** and add ten cows if the contract goes.
feel: **Unsettled**, like a weather change you can smell but not see.
S1.quote: The first ones in pay the most and the last ones in get it cheap.
fieldNote: She sees the danger through the **buyer's AI**, not through anything on her own farm.
She relies on her daughter **Katya** for anything digital and feels guilty asking.
Waiting is a **deliberate strategy** for her, not just reluctance.

steps.text: Wait a year or two to see what neighbours adopt
Ask daughter Katya to take on any new online forms
Switch the potato field to grass if the contract is lost

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then robots by 2031. I'd be 63. Ivan 64.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't understand it, and I don't think the people talking about it understand it either. I'd say somebody in government had better have a plan. That's about all I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking AI doesn't touch my cows in 2028, but it does the potato man's buying and the bank's lending decisions. By 2031 the big farms have robots that work all night and sell beef cheaper than we can. With the shed loan still running, I don't see how we last. I think we'd be selling by 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd stop spending on anything that isn't feed or the loan. I'd ask the Morgans whether they'd rent the grazing from 2030, so we have something coming in. And I'd sit Katya and Lydia down on a video call and tell them what we're thinking about the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a bit stupid, like I've missed a train I didn't know was coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ivan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my husband Ivan we can sell the land but we keep the house. He'd go quiet for a day. Then he'd go and grease the baler, because that's what he does when he's upset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with yourselves if you sold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I've never not farmed. Maybe I'd work in the farm shop on the main road, if it's still there and not a robot.

say: I'd say I don't understand it, and I doubt **the people talking** do either.
I'd say the **government** had better have a plan.
think: AI in 2028 changes the **buyer and the bank** before it touches my cows.
With robot farms by 2031 and the **shed loan** running, we'd likely sell by 2032.
do: Stop all spending except **feed and the loan** in the first year.
Ask the **Morgans next door** about renting our grazing from 2030.
Tell both daughters on a **video call** what we plan for the farm.
feel: **Frightened**, and **foolish**, like missing a train she didn't know was coming.
S2.quote: I'd tell my husband Ivan we can sell the land but we keep the house.
fieldNote: She tracks how AI reaches her through **other people's decisions**: buyer and bank.
She expects to **sell the farm** around 2032, with the loan making things worse.
Her plan is **defensive**: cut spending, rent to neighbours, tell the family.

steps.text: Stop all spending except feed and the shed loan
Ask the Morgans to rent the grazing from 2030
Tell Katya and Lydia on a video call about selling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots in 2034. The shed loan would be paid off by then, nearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, at least there's some warning. I'd tell people at the mart to pay down their debts while they can. That's practical advice, not politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's not great but it's not the end. The loan finishes in 2032. If we can just get there, we own the shed, and then robots come in 2034 when I'm 66. We'd have been thinking of stopping anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw every spare penny at the shed loan to finish it a year early. I'd keep the cows going but not replace the old ones, so the herd shrinks to about thirty by 2033. And I'd wait and see what the government does before deciding to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's a plan in it. I like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the spare pennies come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the newspaper and keep the heating at seventeen. Ivan would do the hedges himself instead of paying the contractor. That's maybe £1,500 a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the potato contract went in 2031 when the AI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it goes. We'd plant grass and live on the cows and my pension when it comes. It'd be tight. It's always tight.

say: I'd say at least there's **some warning** this time.
I'd tell farmers at the mart to **pay down debts** while they can.
think: The **shed loan** finishes in 2032, before robots arrive in 2034.
Robots at 66 land near when we'd **planned to stop** anyway.
do: Put every spare penny into **finishing the loan** a year early.
Let the herd **shrink to about thirty** by not replacing old cows.
Wait for the **government's plan** before deciding to sell.
S3.quote: Ivan would do the hedges himself instead of paying the contractor. That's maybe £1,500 a year.
fieldNote: The **loan end date** is her anchor: five years lets her clear it first.
Her savings come from **small cuts**: the paper, the heating, hedge cutting.
She stays **wait-and-see** on selling, true to her resistant nature.

steps.text: Overpay the shed loan to finish it a year early
Let the herd shrink to thirty by not replacing old cows
Wait for the government's plan before deciding to sell

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2039 for the robots. I'd be 71 and probably done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a problem for the next lot, and I'd mean it kindly. I'd tell the young farmers at the mart to watch it. That's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the robots come after we've stopped. What worries me is still the same: the loan, the potato man, and that nobody takes the farm. Ten years from now we'll be selling or renting it out either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as we are. I'd talk to the girls properly, not on a rush call, about what happens to the farm and whether either of them wants the house. I'd let things go as they go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sad, if anything. Not about robots. About the farm ending with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to happen to the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a young family on the farm, really. Not a company with robots. I'd sell to whoever pays, because we need the money to live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I know. I'd want one thing and do the other. That's life, isn't it? You don't always get to choose.

say: I'd say it's a problem for **the next lot**, kindly meant.
I'd tell young farmers at the mart to **watch it**.
think: Robots come **after we've stopped**, so they don't touch us.
The **loan**, the potato buyer and **no successor** remain our worries.
do: Keep the **farm running** as it is now.
Talk properly with both daughters about **the farm and house**.
Let the sale decision **wait** until we stop.
feel: **Sad** about the farm ending with them, not about robots.
S4.quote: I'd want a young family on the farm, really. Not a company with robots. I'd sell to whoever pays, because we need the money to live.
fieldNote: Ten years puts robots **beyond her working life**; old pressures keep her anxious.
She names an honest **contradiction**: wanting a young family but selling to the highest bidder.
Her feelings are about **the farm ending**, not about technology.

steps.text: Keep running the suckler herd and potato field as now
Talk with both daughters about the farm and the house
Leave the sale decision until the day they stop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the loan would still be running when the robots came. What would help is the bank giving farmers like us a longer time to pay, and somebody plain who'd explain what's really happening, without selling us anything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the farm after us. That's the thing nobody talks about. The robots might not take my job, because I'll be too old by then, but the robots will decide who buys the land.

headlineQuote: The robots might not take my job, because I'll be too old by then, but the robots will decide who buys the land.
portrait: Nora, 58, runs an inherited **90-acre farm** with her husband Ivan: suckler cows, potatoes and hay.
She carries a **£60,000 shed loan**, about two weeks of savings and no successor.
She never uses AI; her daughter Katya does the **online forms**.
She thinks practically, avoids arguments, and **waits** to see what others do.
Her mood hinges on the **loan end date**: alarmed at two years, anxious otherwise.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robot farms arriving while the shed **loan** still runs.
whatWouldHelp: **Longer repayment** terms from the bank for small farmers.
Someone **plain and honest** to explain what's really happening, without selling anything.
